question: What is the institutional tape telling us across 1W, 1D, and 4H timeframes, and why is chasing McKesson at $1,069.43 poor risk-reward compared with waiting for a $940–$985 pullback?

epigraph.quote: A great company in a Stage 2 uptrend still punishes buyers who chase three weeks past the buyable pivot.
epigraph.author: Stage Analysis Desk Principle

web_blocks.title: Why Chasing $1,069.43 Fails the Asymmetry Test (and Options Confirm It)

web_blocks.html: Good companies become bad trades when entry math breaks down. Buying MCK at $1,069.43 against our $857.69 structural stop (below the rising 30W SMA at $870.67 and 200D SMA at $879.78) risks $211.74 per share [24]. Upside to our $1,200.00 base target is $130.57. That yields a dismal 0.62:1 reward-to-risk ratio. In a market Downtrend with 10 distribution days, stretched leaders often pull back 8% to 12% to their rising 50-day moving average without breaking trend.

The options market also shows zero edge in chasing here. Our options desk flags NO_OPTIONS_EDGE. A $1,060/$1,120 call spread costs $27.65 for a $32.35 max gain, or 1.17:1 reward-to-risk—below our 1.25:1 minimum. By contrast, waiting for a dip into the $940.00–$985.00 shelf (near the $954.05 swing low and $974.32 50-day SMA) cuts risk to $127.31 at $985.00 [24]. Upside expands to $215.00, giving a clean 1.69:1 asymmetry ratio.

web_blocks.title: ATR Volatility Math & Why Pullbacks to the 50D SMA Are Routine
paragraphs: McKesson's 14-day Average True Range (ATR) is $25.95 (~2.4% of CMP), with Bollinger Band width at 17.5% [24]. A normal 3-to-4 ATR dip in a Downtrend equals $78 to $104 per share. That lands MCK right inside $965–$991 around the rising 50D SMA ($974.32) [24].

4H momentum is already cooling (4H RSI (51.47), intraday_4h_turn: false), and 1W RSI (71.10) sits in overbought territory [24]. Buyers should let normal volatility bring MCK to the $940–$985 shelf instead of chasing at $1,069.43.

web_blocks.html: Key pivot levels support the same patience. Overhead resistance sits at the 52-week high of $1,121.50 (near pivot R2 at $1,117.66), while minor support sits at $1,045.53 (20-day SMA) [24]. Deeper support sits at the 20-day swing low ($954.05), the rising 50-day SMA ($974.32), and pivot S1 ($907.19) [24]. The primary Stage 2 floor rests at the 30-week SMA ($870.67) and 200-day SMA ($879.78) [24]. Respecting those shelves prevents early entries during market distribution.

Staging entries across $940.00–$985.00 also protects against whipsaw in a Downtrend. A disciplined buyer can put half the position near the rising 50-day SMA ($974.32–$985.00) once 4H momentum turns up [24]. The second half can wait for a deeper test of $940.00–$954.05, with the whole stake guarded by the $857.69 structural stop [24].

If MCK instead breaks above $1,121.50 without dipping, we still refuse to chase [24]. We would only revisit a breakout after a tight multi-week base cools 1W RSI below 65 and S&P 500 breadth exits Downtrend. Patience keeps our capital safe.

book_paragraphs: Chapter 7 told us what McKesson is worth. Chapter 8 asks a very different question: is today, at $1,069.43, the right moment to put fresh cash to work? To answer honestly, we must check both the market weather outside and McKesson's footprint on the chart.

First, look at the market weather. On November 20, 2026, the S&P 500 sits in a confirmed Downtrend. Only 40.4% of stocks trade above their 50-day moving average, and desks logged 10 distribution days in 25 sessions. When the tide goes out like that, most stocks sink. McKesson did the exact opposite. Over 63 trading days, it beat the market by +32.04%, and by +22.52% over 28 days [24]. It climbed +39.08% in six months from $723.68 to $1,121.50 [24]. That relative strength during a selloff is no accident. It marks large pension and mutual funds rotating into defensive, cash-rich healthcare compounders.

Now check three timeframes—weekly, daily, and four-hour—inside that Stage 2 uptrend. On the weekly chart, McKesson is in a Stage 2 Markup, +22.86% above its rising 30-week SMA ($870.67) and +6.92% above its 10-week EMA ($1,000.45) [24]. Yet 1W RSI (71.10) has entered overbought territory [24]. On the daily chart, shares closed at $1,069.43 (TradingView $1,069.72), +9.76% above the 50-day SMA ($974.32) and +21.56% above the 200-day SMA ($879.78) [24]. 1D RSI(14) (60.34) sits in healthy territory alongside a 14-day ATR of $25.95 [24]. On the four-hour chart, the rally is catching its breath: 4H RSI (51.47) cooled near the 4H 20-EMA ($1,073.10), with no fresh upward turn yet [24]. Note that while the raw screen outputs a BUY_AT_CMP_NO_FOMO signal, we override it to ACCUMULATE_ON_DIP because of overbought 1W RSI (71.10), the Downtrend market regime (40.4% breadth above 50DMA and 10 distribution days), and 0.62:1 CMP reward-to-risk [24].

Let's translate that volatility into plain dollars. McKesson's 14-day Average True Range is $25.95, or roughly 2.4% a day [24]. In a market Downtrend with 10 distribution days, even top Stage 2 leaders see three-to-four-ATR shakeouts when funds lock in gains. Three to four ATRs off $1,069.43 equals $78 to $104 per share. That drops the stock into $965 to $991, right on the rising 50-day SMA ($974.32) and 20-day swing low ($954.05) [24]. Waiting for that shelf is not wishful thinking; it is simple market math.

Here is where discipline separates compounder gains from emotional FOMO. If you buy at $1,069.43 today, where must your structural stop-loss sit to avoid normal noise? Just below the major weekly and 200-day floor—at $857.69, under the 30-week SMA ($870.67) and 200-day SMA ($879.78) [24]. You are risking $211.74 per share to make $130.57 up to our $1,200.00 base target. Divide $130.57 by $211.74, and your reward-to-risk ratio is just 0.62 to 1. You are risking nearly two dollars to make one.

Even the options market agrees that chasing here is a bad bet. Our options desk checked a $1,060/$1,120 call spread. It costs $27.65 for a $32.35 max gain—a 1.17 to 1 payout that fails our 1.25 to 1 hurdle, earning NO_OPTIONS_EDGE. Near-term resistance at $1,121.50 caps call convexity, making short-dated calls a poor bet [24]. By contrast, waiting for the Downtrend to pull McKesson into $940.00–$985.00 changes the math [24]. Entering at $985.00 against the same $857.69 stop cuts risk to $127.31 and opens $215.00 of upside to $1,200.00. That flips the ratio from 0.62:1 to 1.69:1.

Look at the horizontal price shelves on the chart to see why this zone matters. Overhead resistance sits at the 52-week high of $1,121.50 and pivot R2 at $1,117.66 [24]. Minor support rests at the 20-day SMA ($1,045.53) and 10-week EMA ($1,000.45) [24]. Below that sits our main buy shelf at $940.00–$985.00, backed by pivot S1 at $907.19 [24]. Knowing every shelf in advance removes guesswork when volatility hits.

book_subsections.title: How Institutional Desks Trade Stage 2 Leaders During a Market Downtrend
paragraphs: When the S&P 500 logs 10 distribution days in 25 sessions and only 40.4% of stocks sit above their 50-day line, managers face a trap. They see defensive leaders like McKesson near 52-week highs and feel forced to buy at any price to hide from the storm. Yet those late chases often trap buyers in four-to-eight-week sideways or downward digestions.

Instead of chasing 1W RSI (71.10), disciplined desks map the shelves where mutual funds will step back in. The first minor shelf is the 20-day SMA ($1,045.53) and 10-week EMA ($1,000.45) [24]. Beneath that sits the primary demand zone: $940.00 to $985.00, where the rising 50-day SMA ($974.32) meets the 20-day swing low ($954.05) [24]. If McKesson dips there on light volume and prints a daily or 4H reversal, you buy the same Tier 1 compounder at 1.69:1 reward-to-risk.

What if McKesson refuses to pull back and breaks out above $1,121.50? Even then, we do not chase blindly. We would only revisit a breakout if shares build a tight multi-week base that cools 1W RSI below 65 while S&P 500 breadth exits Downtrend. Until one of those two setups appears, holding cash is the highest-discipline trade.

book_subsections.title: Staging Entries and Reading Volume Confirmation on the Pullback
paragraphs: Once price enters $940.00 to $985.00, execution still matters. Never catch a falling knife on heavy selling volume. Look for volume to dry up as McKesson drifts toward its rising 50-day SMA at $974.32, then watch for 4H RSI (currently 51.47) to turn back above 50 [24]. Putting half your stake near $975.00 to $985.00 and half near $940.00 to $954.05 lets you scale in cleanly without overcommitting on the first touch.

Remember also why our structural stop sits at $857.69 rather than right under the 50-day line. In a volatile Downtrend, stocks often undercut their 50-day SMA by a few percent to clear tight retail stops before resuming higher. Placing your stop at $857.69—below both the 30-week SMA ($870.67) and 200-day SMA ($879.78)—gives the trade room while ensuring you exit if the primary uptrend breaks [24].

book_subsections.title: Relative Strength Divergence: Why Leaders Pull Back Later, Not Never
paragraphs: A common mistake in chart reading is thinking a stock with +32.04% 63-day relative strength cannot drop 8% to 12%. In truth, strong leaders often hit brief air pockets late in a market Downtrend. When S&P 500 breadth sits at 40.4% and 10 distribution days pile up, managers eventually trim winners to raise cash or rebalance weights.

That is why we never confuse relative strength with immunity. McKesson's -1.63% weekly dip and cooling 4H RSI (51.47) show early profit-taking has begun [24]. Keeping limit orders in $940.00 to $985.00 turns that rebalancing from a threat into our entry catalyst.

Compare your emotional state under those two entries. Buy at $1,069.43 on an overbought 1W RSI (71.10), and a routine 9% dip to the 50-day SMA ($974.32) puts you down $95 a share [24]. You start doubting your thesis even though nothing in the business changed. Wait for $940.00–$985.00 instead, and you step in at support with 1.69:1 reward-to-risk and a clear $857.69 stop.

Every gauge on the dashboard—1W RSI (71.10), +9.76% stretch above the 50-day SMA, cooling 4H RSI (51.47), and NO_OPTIONS_EDGE—points the same way [24]. Respect the Stage 2 uptrend and +32.04% relative strength, and wait until price meets the $940.00 to $985.00 shelf.

Finally, avoid using leveraged call spreads to replace patience here. At $1,069.43, the $1,121.50 52-week high sits just 4.9% overhead, so option sellers price upside tightly [24]. Paying $27.65 for a $1,060/$1,120 call spread to make at most $32.35 gives 1.17:1 convexity. A routine 7% dip to the 50-day SMA wipes out most of that spread before expiry. Waiting for common shares at $940.00 to $985.00 removes time decay and restores 1.69:1 reward-to-risk.
